sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising sequences of ordinary vocabulary tokens, any of which may be corrupted and subsequently revised. During training, UDLMs must denoise from a context that may itself be unreliable, whereas masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) always condition on a clean context. This challenging training objective makes UDLMs more FLOP-intensive to train than MDLMs, but it yields stronger downstream reasoning performance. Recently, selective looping, which recursively applies a few early Transformer layers within each denoising step, has been shown to improve training efficiency in MDLMs under an iso-FLOP budget. We investigate looping in UDLMs while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged. We find that looping significantly improves training efficiency: looped UDLMs reach the validation NLL of a non-looped UDLM trained on about 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8x fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3x fewer on FineWeb-Edu. We also find that, at a matched NFE budget, looped UDLMs reach up to 9.8% lower generation perplexity than the non-looped UDLM, with most gains achieved at moderate loop counts. Finally, we study different loop-count distributions and find that sampling smaller loop counts more frequently during training improves inference efficiency: on downstream tasks, this strategy uses 12% fewer loops than uniform loop-count sampling without degrading accuracy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate text by starting from corrupted sequence and denoising many positions in parallel (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2025). The forward process decides whether the denoiser knows which tokens are corrupted. Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) replace corrupted tokens with dedicated mask symbol, so the corrupted positions are always known. Under the standard absorbing-state reverse process, unmasked tokens are never changed (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025). Uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) instead replace tokens with random tokens from the vocabulary, so every position holds an ordinary token that gives no sign of being corrupted (Austin et al., 2021; Schiff et al., 2025; Sahoo et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2026). Because of this, the reverse process can revise any position at any denoising step. The distinction is becoming more important as uniform diffusion is scaled to billion-parameter language models for reasoning (DiffusionGemma Team et al., 2026; Sahoo et al., 2026a). Denoising in UDLMs is harder than in MDLMs because the denoiser must predict corrupted tokens from context that may itself be corrupted. If token does not fit its context, either the token or one of its neighbors was corrupted, and the denoiser has to work out which. At each position it therefore predicts two things. The first is the probability that the observed token was retained, which depends on the noise level and on how well the token agrees with its context. The second is the clean token itself, in case it was replaced. Both are read from the models contextual prediction of the clean token, so refining that prediction 1 Preprint Figure 1: Looping saves training compute on OWT and FineWeb-Edu. Best validation NLL so far against training FLOPs for uniform (left) and FLOP-proportional (right) looping, on OWT (top) and FineWeb-Edu (bottom). should improve both. The most straightforward way to refine it is to scale up the model by adding layers, but this increases the parameter count. Another way is looping, which spends more computation on the same noisy sequence by reusing existing layers, without adding parameters (Dehghani et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2020; Giannou et al., 2023; Geiping et al., 2025). Lee et al. (2026) recently showed that selectively looping small block of early-middle layers improves training efficiency in MDLMs, where unresolved positions are explicitly identified. Whether looping also helps UDLMs, where the denoiser cannot tell which positions are corrupted, remains open. We therefore ask: How useful is looping for UDLM denoising, and how does the loop-count distribution affect training and inference? To investigate this question, we integrate looping into UDLMs while keeping the training objective and sampler unchanged, using DUO++ (Deschenaux et al., 2026), the most efficient recipe for training UDLMs in the literature. Besides the uniform loop-count distribution used in prior work on looped masked diffusion (Lee et al., 2026), we study two alternatives: FLOP-proportional sampling, which gives each loop count the same expected share of training FLOPs, so smaller loop counts are sampled more often, and noise-proportional sampling, which assigns larger loop counts to noisier inputs. At inference, we consider fixed looping, which uses the same loop count at every denoising step, and adaptive looping, which halts once the relative change in the hidden state between consecutive iterations falls below threshold. Main findings. We summarize our observations as follows: 1. Looping makes UDLM training more compute-efficient. Looped UDLMs reach the validation NLL of non-looped UDLM trained on about 0.5 trillion tokens with up to 2.8 fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText (Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019) and 3.3 fewer on FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024). 2. Looping helps at inference. Looped UDLMs reach up to 9.8% lower generative perplexity than the non-looped UDLM at the same number of denoising steps, with most of the gain captured at moderate loop counts. Concretely, UDLM needs more training FLOPs than an MDLM to reach the same validation NLL (Sahoo et al., 2026b). sections.title: 5 Results
sections.content: Where to loop. On OpenWebText (50k steps, one seed), two-block slices starting anywhere in blocks 15 perform about equally, late slices with short tail are clearly worse, and raising Smax beyond 12 gives no further gain (Figure 3a, Appendix E). All looped models therefore loop blocks 12 with Smax = 12. 5.1 Looping is training-compute efficient We compare each looped run with the non-looped baseline at matched training FLOPs on both datasets (Figure 1, with per-step curves in Figure 10). Both looped runs stay below the baseline at every budget, and the savings are larger on FineWeb-Edu than on OpenWebText. Evaluating at = 6, 8, or 12 gives nearly the same curve, so few loop iterations capture almost all of the gain. FLOP-proportional sampling closely matches the final NLL of uniform sampling (3.159 vs. 3.154 on OpenWebText and 3.122 vs. 3.119 on FineWeb-Edu), and it is better at = 1 (3.289 vs. 3.306), the loop count it trains on most often. Finding 1. Looping improves training efficiency in UDLMs. Across OpenWebText and FineWeb-Edu, both looped models reach the non-looped baselines validation NLL with 2.73.3 fewer training FLOPs. Noise-proportional sampling has the same per-step cost as uniform sampling, so the two runs are iso-FLOP at every step. We stopped it after 16 epochs of OpenWebText. Besides fixed loop counts, we score it with band-consistent evaluation, which scores each noise band only at loop counts it was trained on (Appendix B). None of these six evaluations reaches the uniform or FLOP-proportional frontier (Figure 3b), and the other two distributions reach its best NLL with roughly 30% less compute. Finding 2. The noise-proportional distribution offers no benefit. At matched OpenWebText training FLOPs, assigning deeper loops to noisier inputs underperforms uniform and FLOP-proportional sampling (the best result trails FLOP-proportional by +0.029 NLL). This is consistent with Figure 6b, where the loop gain at inference peaks at intermediate diffusion times rather than at the noisiest inputs. 8 Preprint Figure 5: Where adaptive looping stops (ϵ = 0.1, Smax = 12). sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Discrete diffusion language models. Discrete diffusion models use structured categorical corruption (Austin et al., 2021; Hoogeboom et al., 2021), with much of the literature focusing on masked diffusion (Sahoo et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025; Lou et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025). UDLMs instead corrupt tokens into ordinary vocabulary tokens, allowing previously generated tokens to be revised (Schiff et al., 2025; Sahoo et al., 2025; 2026b). Existing acceleration methods largely reduce the number of denoising steps through improved sampling or distillation (Song et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2025; Israel et al., 2025; Luxembourg et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2025). Our work instead studies recurrent computation within each denoising step, leaving the diffusion objective and sampler unchanged. Looped transformers. Shared-weight recurrence increases effective depth without adding parameters, building on Universal Transformers, equilibrium models, and parameter-shared architectures (Dehghani et al., 2019; Bai et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2020; Giannou et al., 2023). Recent work studies iterative computation, test-time scaling, and the qualitycompute tradeoffs of recurrent depth (Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; McLeish et al., 2025; Prairie et al., 2026; Schwethelm et al., 2026). We investigate these questions in UDLM denoisers, including how recurrent depth should be sampled during training. Looped diffusion denoisers. Closest to our work, Lee et al. (2026) study recurrent depth in masked diffusion, while related approaches explore recursive blocks and fixed-point formulations (Carballo-Castro et al., 2026; Miele et al., 2026). In standard absorbing masked diffusion, revealed tokens remain fixed, whereas UDLMs must denoise observations of uncertain reliability and can revise any token between diffusion steps. We study whether recurrence remains effective under this different corruption structure, and how its computation should be allocated. Recurrence across denoising steps. Self-conditioning reuses clean-token predictions across diffusion steps (Chen et al., 2023; Strudel et al., 2022; Dieleman et al., 2022). Related approaches propagate latent states across steps or introduce additional denoising 11 Preprint recursion (Jo et al., 2026; Suleymanzade et al., 2026; Yoo et al., 2026; Cameron et al., 2026). Our approach instead loops slice of transformer blocks within each denoiser evaluation, updating hidden representations while keeping the noisy sequence and diffusion time fixed. These directions are complementary.

sections.title: 7 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: We studied the effect of looping in UDLMs by repeating two-block slice of the denoiser and training it with random loop counts. Looped models reach the validation NLL of the non-looped baseline with up to 2.8 fewer training FLOPs on OpenWebText and 3.3 fewer on FineWeb-Edu. We show that at inference, looping lowers generative perplexity by up to 9.8% at the same NFE and zero-shot perplexity by 11.5% on average. With adaptive looping, the model needs 2635% fewer loop iterations on multiple-choice tasks and keeps the same accuracy. Training on lower loop counts more often helps further: on the same tasks, the model needs 12% fewer loop iterations than with uniform sampling, without degrading accuracy. We plan to extend this study by comparing how looping helps masked and uniform diffusion, especially on reasoning tasks. sections.content: Every run uses the same configuration  (Table 4)  . Figure 10 shows the training curves. Pretraining datasets. We train on OpenWebText (OWT) (Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019) and on the sample-10BT configuration of FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024) (9,672,101 documents, nominally 10B tokens). In both cases we hold out the last 100,000 documents for validation and train on the rest. We tokenize with the GPT-2 tokenizer (V = 50,257), put an EOS between documents, and pack the stream into 1,024-token sequences made of BOS, 1,022 payload tokens, and EOS. Packing is done separately for each batch of 1,000 documents, and the leftover tokens of each batch are discarded.
